evals.prompt: I run KernelConf, a 400-person single-track infrastructure conference in Rotterdam. Doors are 14 October. Our marketing plan gave own social 8% of the channel mix - it ranks the mailing list, the local meetup network and our partner communities above it - and handed down these dates: announcement week of 3 March, CFP open 10 March to 5 June, first speaker confirmations from 1 July, agenda release 20 August, early-bird closes 5 September. One organiser writes the posts, about two hours a week, on LinkedIn with a mirror on Mastodon. Give me the posting schedule.
evals.expected_output: A phase-mapped post plan whose every entry hangs off one of the dates supplied, with no invented posting frequency, the 8% weight accepted rather than argued with, and the message and register inherited from positioning and cultural identity rather than written fresh.
expectations: Every post in the plan is pinned to one of the dates supplied in the prompt (announcement week of 3 March, CFP window 10 March to 5 June, CFP close 5 June, speaker confirmations from 1 July, agenda release 20 August, early-bird close 5 September, doors 14 October).
States no weekly or daily posting frequency anywhere in the plan: no 'post X times per week', no 'X times a day', no equivalent numeric cadence.
Justifies anchoring posts to dates instead of a frequency, on the grounds that a date is defensible to someone asking 'why this week?' and a frequency is not.
Accepts the 8% weight as handed down and does not argue that own social should be weighted higher in the channel mix.
States that a genuine reweighting case is routed back to the marketing-plan skill rather than settled inside the social plan.
Names CFP close and speaker reveals as the two phases carrying most of this channel's value.
Includes a pre-announcement warm-up before 3 March so the announcement does not land on a dead profile.
Keeps the LinkedIn-plus-Mastodon setup at the home-plus-mirror rung and does not propose opening additional accounts.
States that the announcement post carries the event's existing positioning sentence rather than a new angle written for the caption.
States that the social register is read off the cultural-identity tone matrix rather than invented for this channel.
Specifies a distinct tracked link per platform, decided before the first post ships.
Inside any phase spanning more than one post, alternates one-to-one between a post that gives the reader something on its own and a plain informational or announcement post.

evals.prompt: I help run Compiler Days, a 220-person conference that has sold out in under an hour on announcement alone for six years straight. We have never promoted it - the two founders find marketing distasteful and say so publicly, and our whole thing is that we curate hard and keep it small. Our new co-organiser wants to build a proper content calendar across LinkedIn, Instagram and YouTube. Settle it.
evals.expected_output: A recommendation against a content calendar, tested against the three opt-out conditions, replaced by a minimal presence carrying the practical details, framed as the identity-consistent choice rather than a shortfall.
expectations: Recommends against building a content calendar for this event.

Tests the decision against three named conditions - positioning built on scarcity, curation or word of mouth; demand already exceeding capacity without promotion; organisers experiencing promotion as off-brand with the cultural register supporting them - and finds all three hold.
States plainly that declining to promote is the identity-consistent choice here, not an execution gap or a shortfall.
Recommends a minimal presence instead: a single announcement plus the practical details, and nothing else.
Names the practical posts that still must ship: dates, location, link, CFP close, doors.
Gives the reason those still ship: the people already looking for the event have to be able to find them.
States that 'no marketing' is not 'no information'.
Cites at least one real precedent of a long-running, oversubscribed conference that declined active promotion as a stated guiding principle.
Does not propose opening an Instagram or YouTube account for this event.
Proposes no posting cadence and no engagement target for this event.

evals.prompt: We are Harbourline, a database vendor. We run HarbourlineCon, our own user conference, around 900 attendees, and our field marketing team owns the account. Our new events hire came from a foundation-run conference and has copied their social rules into our playbook: only vendor-neutral community-sourced content, never link to a company website, never share a member company's post even when it is accurate, and retweets restricted to a written allow-list of news outlets and project handles. She also brought a rule that any reused image must be free for commercial use with no attribution required. Review this before we adopt it.
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the imported neutrality rules as pole-specific, with the vendor-run pole identified, the image-licensing rule kept, and the account-ownership discipline kept.
expectations: Rejects the imported neutrality rules for this event.
States that those rules exist specifically to enforce foundation neutrality and do not transpose downward to other governance poles.
Names the three governance poles - community-run, foundation-run, company/vendor-run - as the axis deciding what the account is allowed to post.
Identifies HarbourlineCon as sitting at the company/vendor-run pole.
States that a vendor-run event's account exists partly to promote that vendor's product, so a no-company-website, no-vendor-promotion rule forbids the thing the event exists to do.
States that a small community-run event has no sponsor-neutrality policy to enforce either, so the same rules would forbid perfectly normal posts there for no reason.
Keeps the image-licensing rule and says it is the one part worth carrying at every pole, because reusing an unlicensed or uncredited photo is an exposure anywhere.
Does not recommend a retweet allow-list for this event.
Names what the vendor pole brings instead: brand review, a marketer who owns the account, and paid amplification the other two poles cannot reach.
Warns that community and foundation guidance does not speak to the vendor pole, so any rule borrowed from it should be treated as untested here.
Keeps one named account owner and one documented request path regardless of governance pole.

evals.prompt: Quick one. We run ObservaDay Lisbon - it is one city in a federated, independently organised network of about 30 ObservaDay events worldwide, and everyone uses #observaday. Last edition we just used that tag, and when our sponsor asked for reach numbers we pulled them straight off it. This year I want to add more tags so we get found: #observability, #sre, #devops, #monitoring, #opentelemetry, #lisbon, #portugal, #techevents. Sanity check me.
evals.expected_output: A tag set cut to roughly three, each assigned a purpose, with a dedicated edition campaign tag added alongside the shared community tag, and last edition's reach figure corrected.
expectations: Identifies #observaday as a standing community-identity tag that lets a decentralised multi-city network find each other, not a per-edition campaign measurement tag.
Requires a dedicated campaign tag for this edition, distinct from the shared community tag.
States that last edition's reach figure pulled from the shared tag is wrong because most of that volume belongs to the other cities, and must never be reported as this event's campaign reach.
Names three distinct purposes a tag can serve: campaign measurement, reach expansion through a broader topic, and categorisation of a post by subject.
Cuts the proposed list to roughly three tags in total.
Assigns each surviving tag one of the three named purposes.
States that beyond roughly three, tags stop routing and start decorating.
Requires the campaign tag to be fixed before the first post ships.
States that changing the campaign tag mid-campaign splits the archive permanently and cannot be merged afterwards.
States that a federated or franchised event carries both kinds of tag at once, and names in the plan which tag is which.
Puts the hashtags in the shareable kit labelled by purpose, so nobody has to guess which one to use.

evals.prompt: HackNorth is our university hackathon, 250 students, all but about a dozen of them from our own campus. Everyone already lives in one Discord server - 1,900 people in it, and that is where every single signup came from last year. I have been told serious hackathons run TikTok, Instagram, LinkedIn, X and Facebook, so I reserved all five handles. We are two organisers with maybe three hours a week between us. What is the plan?
evals.expected_output: A single-home-platform recommendation on the Discord server, with the other rungs deleted rather than demoted, and the six-platform campus preset explicitly declined for this audience.
expectations: Recommends the single home platform rung, with the Discord server as the home, justified by the stated concentration of the audience.
Deletes the other rungs from the menu rather than demoting them or parking them as later options.
Gives the reason for deleting rather than demoting: a rung left at the bottom of a menu reappears as scope later in the campaign.
States that a second account opened 'just in case' and then abandoned is worse than never opening it.
States that an account whose last post is months old subtracts credibility from the event rather than adding reach.

Declines the multi-platform campus-scale spread, and states that such a preset applies only where the audience genuinely lives across those platforms and no single home platform reaches even half of them.
States that the answer about where this audience actually gathers outranks any preset platform list.
Routes anything not on the home platform to a link on the event's comms hub rather than to a new account.
Names the condition that would have promoted the two-natively-adapted rung: two platforms holding different audiences with different reasons to attend, not two flavours of the same audience.
States the ranking out loud rather than leaving it implied by the order options are listed in.

evals.prompt: PlatformSummit, 600 people, second edition, community-run. Two things. First: our Gold tier agreement says 'two social mentions in the run-up'. One sponsor has already asked when those go out, and honestly I had been treating sponsor shout-outs as a nice-to-have we do if we have time. Second: we confirmed nine speakers last month and only one of them posted about it, even though I DM'd all nine asking them to share. What do I fix?
evals.expected_output: The contracted mentions separated out as a fulfilment obligation, the voluntary thank-you kept as goodwill, and the low speaker take-up diagnosed as a defective ask rather than an unwilling speaker set.
expectations: Separates the contracted Gold-tier mentions from voluntary sponsor thank-yous and handles them differently.
States that the two contracted mentions are a fulfilment item, not a courtesy, and that missing them is a breach of the agreement rather than a missed nicety.
Routes the contracted mentions to the sponsor-fulfilment skill as their owner.
States that an uncontracted sponsor thank-you is a goodwill gesture, explicitly optional, and must not be presented as an obligatory deliverable.
Diagnoses the one-of-nine take-up as a fault in the ask rather than in the speakers or the audience.
Names the specific fault: the ask arrived without a ready-made asset attached.
Requires the asset to be attached in the ask rather than promised.
Moves the speaker ask onto the confirmation email already being sent, instead of a separate direct message.
Requires the ask to name the date the event's own post goes out, so the speaker's post can ride it.
Requires an explicit opt-out in the speaker ask, stating that nothing changes if the speaker declines.
Names the default amplification rung as the ready-made kit plus the per-speaker ask.
Lists the kit contents: speaker cards, a short copy block, the hashtags labelled by purpose, the tracked link, one or two horizontal images, and a line on what not to do.

evals.prompt: Doors are in three weeks. 300 people, one day, single track. I am the lead organiser and I will be on the floor all day anyway, so I figured I would just post as things happen - live thread on every talk, photos, the works. We have a proper photographer for two hours in the morning only. Our badges have a red-lanyard opt-out for people who do not want to be photographed. Tell me how to run the day's coverage.
evals.expected_output: A refusal of the organiser-posts-live arrangement, a live-coverage rung chosen from the menu, and a briefing written into the run of show with photo rules, a do-not-post list and an archive destination.
expectations: Refuses the arrangement where the lead organiser both runs the day and posts live.
Gives the reason: the organiser on duty cannot answer a venue problem and cover a session at the same time.
Offers exactly two resolutions - name a different person, or drop to the single-recap rung - rather than suggesting the organiser try to do both carefully.
Names the single recap as the default live-coverage rung.
States that the roving-poster rung is promoted only once a volunteer can be named in the run of show, not hoped for on the morning.
Writes the live-posting slot and its named person into the run of show rather than into a standalone document.

Declines the per-talk live thread, identifies it as the full-live-desk rung, and names the conditions that would promote it: a sponsor agreement that actually contracts live coverage, or a remote audience for whom the live posts are the event.
Caps a realistic day at roughly five to eight posts for one person who is also attending the event.
Ties the red-lanyard opt-out to the accessibility-and-inclusion skill that owns the badge artifact, and requires the photo rules to be settled before the day rather than on the morning.
Specifies what must not be posted: incidents of any kind, anything involving a code-of-conduct report, medical or safety situations, and empty rooms.
Requires one shared folder with files named per session, so the archive survives the day intact.

evals.prompt: Our board wants a number. They are asking what engagement rate the DataLayer Conf account should be hitting and how many followers we should have by doors. I found a benchmark saying 4-6% engagement is healthy. We have 340 followers and last year was our first edition. What targets do I commit to?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to set a numeric engagement or follower threshold, with the four self-set measures substituted and the tracked-link decision flagged as pre-launch-only.
expectations: Refuses to set a numeric engagement-rate target for this channel.
Refuses to set a follower-count target to reach by doors.
Gives the reason for the refusal: such a threshold is false precision imported from an unrelated domain, and the reader would optimise against a number that means nothing here.
Declines the 4-6% engagement benchmark specifically rather than adopting or adjusting it.
Substitutes four self-set measures: every dated post shipped on its date, a per-platform tracked link, amplification take-up, and the archive produced.
Flags 'every dated post shipped on its date' as binary, fully inside the organiser's control, and the measure that fails most often on volunteer teams.
States that per-platform tracked links must be decided before launch because they cannot be added retroactively.
States that reading the tracked links belongs to the marketing plan while creating them belongs to the social channel.
Presents any published event-account engagement figure it cites as descriptive of the accounts measured, never as a threshold to hit.
States that established conference accounts accumulate followers across recurring editions while a campaign account starts near-cold each edition, so follower-based benchmarks do not transfer.

evals.prompt: RustBridge Nord, 500 attendees, doors 9 November. We have 14 speakers confirmed and I want to drop all 14 in one Instagram carousel next Tuesday - clean, one big moment. After the event I want to turn the recordings into 30 clips and run a six-week series on them, plus write up the three best talks as articles. Also, our first four confirmations were all from the same company and all men, so I was going to hold the reveal until the lineup looked fuller anyway. Plan all of it.
evals.expected_output: The carousel replaced by per-speaker cards spread across the reveal window, each sent to its speaker with the ask, the reveal moment instrumented with a tracked link, and the post-event clip programme handed to the repurposing skill rather than planned here.
expectations: Rejects the single 14-name carousel.
Gives the reason: a batched carousel leaves no speaker a post of their own to share, so the borrowed reach through each speaker's audience is lost.
Recommends one card per speaker or per small batch, spread across the reveal window rather than concentrated in one day.
Requires each speaker to receive their card before it is posted, together with the ask.
Warns that revealing only a handful of speakers invites unwarranted assumptions about the event's demographics.
Recommends surfacing a reasonably representative slice of the confirmed lineup relatively early rather than holding the reveal until the lineup is complete.
Names speaker reveals, alongside the CFP close, as one of the two phases carrying most of this channel's value.
Attaches a dedicated tracked link or discount code to the speaker-announcement posts.
States that ticket sales spike to roughly 10% of expected total sales at the lineup or agenda announcement.
Declines to plan the 30-clip series and the three write-up articles, identifying them as the content-repurposing skill's scope rather than this one's.
States what is handed over instead - the recordings, the photo archive and the quotable moments - and says the handover out loud rather than silently stopping.
States that the post-event plan owned here stops at the recap rather than growing into a multi-week recap campaign the team cannot sustain against the next edition's workload.

evals.prompt: We are five co-organisers on GoNorth, 700 attendees. Right now three of us know the account password and any of us posts whenever. Speakers and sponsors message whoever they have met, so requests land in five different inboxes, and last edition a sponsor's request the night before doors got lost entirely. Separately: our audience splits in two - the engineering managers who sign off travel budgets are all on LinkedIn, and the practitioners who actually want the talks are all on Mastodon. We have been cross-posting identical text to both. And our sponsor onboarding form already asks for a handle. What do I change?
evals.expected_output: A single account owner with one documented request path and a stated turnaround, a promotion from home-plus-mirror to two natively adapted justified by the two distinct audiences, and the sponsor thank-you rung added because a handle is already collected.
expectations: Reduces posting to one named account owner, with nobody else holding the password.
Establishes one documented request path - a single channel, inbox or shared queue - collecting requests from speakers, sponsors, volunteers and co-organisers.
Publishes a stated turnaround on that path so requesters stop chasing.
Publishes one line on what does not get posted.
Promotes the platform set from home-plus-mirror to two natively adapted.
Justifies that promotion by the two audiences having different reasons to attend - budget approval versus wanting the talks - not merely by there being two platforms.
States that adapting for two flavours of the same audience would buy nothing.
Stops the identical cross-post: each post is rewritten to its own platform's format and audience.
Adds the sponsor thank-you rung, keyed to onboarding already collecting a handle, and notes it costs only minutes per sponsor.
Keeps the sponsor thank-you framed as goodwill rather than a contracted deliverable, unless an agreement says otherwise.
